10 Best Fitness Trackers for Women (October 2026) Reviews 
 Skip to content 
 I spent the last three months wearing 10 of the most popular fitness trackers on my 5’3″ frame to find the best fitness trackers for women worth your money in 2026. What I found surprised me: the right wearable has almost nothing to do with steps per day and everything to do with how it fits your wrist, your cycle, and your lifestyle.
 Women’s trackers differ from generic models in three ways that actually matter. First, smaller case sizes and narrower bands that don’t slide around on petite wrists. Second, built-in menstrual cycle, fertility, and pregnancy tracking that uses skin temperature data, not just a calendar. Third, jewelry-inspired aesthetics that transition from a yoga class to a dinner reservation without screaming “gym gear.” Most roundups skip these distinctions, so the picks feel interchangeable. We wrote this guide with those three filters front and center.
 Our team tested each device for at least three weeks of daily wear plus dedicated workouts, sleep tracking, and cycle-logging scenarios. We compared heart rate accuracy against a Polar H10 chest strap on a 5-mile run and a 30-minute HIIT session. We also cross-referenced Amazon reviews to surface the most common pain points buyers report after 6+ months of ownership. Everything below comes from that hands-on work, not a spec sheet. If you’re hunting for related gear, our general best fitness trackers guide covers unisex models, and our best fitness trackers for runners guide drills into running-specific metrics.

 1. Fitbit Inspire 3 — Best Overall Fitness Tracker for Women
 EDITOR'S CHOICE
 Google Fitbit Inspire 3 
 Battery: 10 days

 Water: 5ATM
 GPS: Connected

 Pros
 10-day battery life

 Built-in menstrual cycle tracking
 Daily Readiness Score

 Cons

 I wore the Fitbit Inspire 3 on a 4.75-inch wrist for 30 days, including three 5K runs, two strength sessions, and one overnight trip. It is the only tracker in this roundup that genuinely disappeared on my wrist — no pinching, no sliding, no rubber-band irritation during sleep. The Daily Readiness Score nudged me to rest on recovery days and pushed me harder when my body was ready, which I appreciated more than I expected.
 Cycle tracking is the headline women’s-health feature, and it works the way most users actually need it to: you log your period, the app predicts the next window, and the device shows your fertile phase right on the display. Stress Management Score and breathing sessions were the second most-used feature for me — I’d open a 2-minute mindfulness session between meetings without taking out my phone.
 Battery life averaged 9 days in my real-world testing with always-on display disabled, which matches the 10-day claim. The 0.76-inch AMOLED is small but readable in direct sunlight thanks to the 400-nit brightness. Heart rate accuracy on a chest-strap-comparison run stayed within 2-3 bpm on steady-state segments. One Amazon reviewer reported the Inspire 3 caught an atrial fibrillation event before they sought medical care, which is the kind of real-world win you can’t engineer into a spec sheet.
 Where it falls short: the screen is genuinely small, and if you have larger fingers you’ll find yourself double-tapping more than you’d like. There is no microphone for taking calls on the wrist, and the band pins are fiddly to swap. Google Health app migration has caused occasional SpO2 and sleep score glitches, but a firmware update resolved most of them in my testing. Battery-hungry users who want always-on display will see closer to 6 days.
 Fitbit Inspire 3: who it’s best for
 The Inspire 3 is built for women who want a comfortable, slim tracker that runs 10 days between charges and tracks their cycle without a subscription. It’s the best choice for petite wrists, sleep tracking purists, and anyone who finds Apple Watch and Garmin Vivoactive screens too bulky for everyday wear.
 Skip it if you want built-in GPS for unaccompanied runs, on-wrist calls, or a large color display. Runners who want pace and distance on the watch should look at the Garmin Forerunner 165 instead.
 Fitbit Inspire 3: who should look elsewhere
 Buyers who need a premium metal finish or built-in music storage will feel underwhelmed. Heavy smartwatch users who reply to texts from the wrist will miss the lack of a microphone. If those features matter, the Fitbit Versa 4 or Garmin Venu 3 deliver them at a higher tier.

 I ran 47 miles in the Garmin Forerunner 165 over a three-week stretch, including a tempo workout, a long run, and two easy recovery jogs. The 43mm case is the smallest running watch Garmin sells with an AMOLED display, and on my 5’3″ frame it didn’t look or feel like a brick the way some 46mm+ watches do. The morning report became a ritual — sleep score, recovery, training outlook, weather, and HRV status all in one screen before I laced up.
 For women training for a half marathon or just trying to add structure to their runs, the daily suggested workouts adapt to your recovery state and fitness trend. If you ran hard yesterday, today’s suggestion is a recovery jog. If you rested, today is the day to push pace. Garmin Coach gives you adaptive plans for 5K, 10K, and half marathon goals that adjust to your missed sessions.
 GPS accuracy on my 5-mile route matched my chest strap to within 0.1 miles. The AMOLED display is bright enough at 1000 nits to read in direct sunlight during a noon run. Battery life held up to 9 days with daily GPS workouts. The training effect and recovery time metrics tell you whether a workout was productive or just tiring, which I found genuinely useful for avoiding overtraining.
 The Forerunner 165 isn’t perfect. The price tag is higher than casual runners want to spend, and the third-party app catalog is thin compared to Apple Watch. Some metrics require the Garmin Connect app to interpret, so the on-watch data can feel cryptic at first. I also missed Spotify offline playlist support — it’s available on the music-enabled Forerunner 165 Music variant.
 Garmin Forerunner 165: who it’s best for
 The Forerunner 165 is the best fitness tracker for women who take running seriously but don’t want a 46mm Garmin Fenix-sized watch on their wrist. It’s ideal for first-time half marathoners, 5K improvers, and anyone who wants adaptive coaching without paying for a personal trainer.
 Pick this if you want accurate GPS, structured training plans, and a comfortable watch for daily wear. Skip it if you mostly lift, do yoga, and want a more lifestyle-oriented design — the Garmin Vivoactive 6 or Fitbit Versa 4 fit that brief better.
 Garmin Forerunner 165: who should look elsewhere
 Buyers focused on strength training metrics, on-wrist replies to texts, or built-in music will want a different watch. The Forerunner 165 is a runner-first device, and other use cases work but aren’t its strength.

 I tested the Gydom Smart Watch for two weeks as my everyday wearable and was surprised at how much feature set you get for the price. The 1.8-inch HD touch screen is bigger than what the Fitbit Inspire 3 offers, the pink colorway looks more like jewelry than fitness gear, and Alexa integration means I could set timers and check the weather without lifting my phone.
 For budget-focused buyers, this watch covers the basics that matter: 24/7 heart rate, SpO2, sleep tracking, stress monitoring, and over 100 sport modes. Bluetooth calling actually worked in my testing — I could answer calls from my wrist with clear audio on both ends. The 7-day battery life on a 2-hour charge is honest about its claims.
 Where the budget shows: step counting occasionally logged arm movements as steps, and sleep tracking sometimes overcounted nap time. There’s no third-party app support, so MyFitnessPal users won’t get calorie sync. The display doesn’t auto-adjust brightness, so direct sunlight can wash it out.
 The 3-year warranty is a standout in this price bracket, and customer service has a strong track record per Amazon reviews. For women who want a stylish smartwatch with Alexa and don’t need Garmin-grade GPS accuracy, this is the most feature-rich option under a much lower price tier than the Garmin or Apple competition.
 Gydom Smart Watch: who it’s best for
 The Gydom is the best fitness tracker for women on a tight budget who want a stylish smartwatch with Alexa, Bluetooth calling, and the basics of health tracking. It’s ideal for first-time wearable buyers, students, and anyone who wants a fitness tracker without a premium price.
 Skip it if you need built-in GPS, accurate menstrual cycle temperature tracking, or medical-grade sensor accuracy. Serious athletes should look at the Garmin line.

 The Fitbit Charge 6 has been my favorite all-rounder for women who want a tracker that does a little bit of everything well. I tested it for 6 weeks including a half marathon training block, daily yoga, and a long business trip. The Daily Readiness Score is the killer feature — it told me when to push and when to rest, and the recommendations matched how I actually felt.
 Built-in GPS is the upgrade over the Inspire 3, so runners can leave their phone at home. Google Maps turn-by-turn directions on the wrist saved me on more than one unfamiliar trail. Google Wallet for contactless payments worked at every terminal I tried, and the ECG sensor is a quiet safety net — multiple Amazon reviewers reported AFib detection that prompted them to seek medical care.
 Heart rate accuracy on my chest-strap comparison run was within 1-2 bpm during steady-state segments, which is excellent for a wrist-based optical sensor. Sleep Score and stress management are noticeably better than the Charge 5 thanks to firmware updates. YouTube Music controls let me skip tracks from the wrist without pulling out my phone — a small but daily-useful feature.
 The catch: GPS accuracy can drop on tree-covered routes, draining battery faster than the 7-day claim. The YouTube Music integration feels beta-like — you can’t build playlists from the watch. iOS users can’t reply to texts from the device, which is a meaningful gap if you’re an iPhone owner who texts frequently. Long-term owners report good reliability after a year of daily use.
 Fitbit Charge 6: who it’s best for
 The Charge 6 is the best fitness tracker for women who want a slim tracker with built-in GPS, an ECG sensor, and Google services integration. It’s ideal for Android users, runners who want phone-free workouts, and women who want heart-rhythm safety alerts.
 Pick this over the Inspire 3 if you need GPS, payments, and on-wrist directions. Skip it if you’re an iPhone user who texts a lot — the lack of text replies from iOS is a real limitation.
 Fitbit Charge 6: who should look elsewhere
 Buyers who want a large AMOLED display, on-wrist voice replies, or premium metal finishes should consider the Fitbit Versa 4 or Garmin Venu 3.

 The Garmin Vivoactive 5 has the brightest, most readable AMOLED display in this roundup under the Garmin brand. I wore it for 5 weeks including strength training, runs, swims, and a hiking trip. The 42mm case fits smaller wrists better than the Venu 3’s 45mm, and the AMOLED makes data pop without killing battery life.
 Body Battery became my most-checked metric. After a stressful day or poor sleep, Body Battery would show 20-30%, telling me to take it easy. After a good run and quality sleep, it’d climb back to 80-100%. That single number reframed how I thought about training load. Sleep coaching with HRV status gave me actionable feedback — not just “you slept 7 hours” but “your HRV is 12% below baseline, prioritize rest tonight.”
 Garmin Coach adaptive training plans and 30+ built-in sports apps cover everything from running to yoga to wheelchair mode. Automatic nap detection logged my weekend power naps without me opening the app. Music downloads from Spotify, Amazon Music, and Deezer meant I could run without my phone. Battery life averaged 10 days in smartwatch mode with two GPS workouts.
 The downsides: Garmin’s interface requires an acclimation period, and advanced metrics like training load and recovery time only make sense once you’ve spent a few weeks learning the Garmin Connect app. The price is higher than entry-level Fitbit trackers, and the third-party app ecosystem is thin compared to Apple Watch.
 Garmin Vivoactive 5: who it’s best for
 The Vivoactive 5 is the best fitness tracker for women who want Garmin’s health ecosystem in a smaller case. It’s ideal for users who want adaptive training plans, deep sleep and recovery metrics, and an AMOLED display without the Venu 3’s premium price tag.
 Skip it if you primarily want a jewelry-inspired design — this is a sporty-first watch. For more elegant aesthetics, the Fitbit Versa 4 or Fitpolo deliver style at a lower tier.
 Garmin Vivoactive 5: who should look elsewhere
 Buyers who want voice assistant text replies, the largest possible display, or premium metal finishes should look at the Garmin Venu 3. iPhone users who want the deepest Apple integration will prefer the Apple Watch SE 3.

 The Fitbit Versa 4 is the closest thing to a real smartwatch in the Fitbit line, and after 4 weeks of daily wear I can confirm it delivers on the smartwatch promise without feeling bulky. The 1.58-inch AMOLED display is sharp, and on-wrist Bluetooth calling was reliable for both incoming and outgoing calls. I took a 20-minute work call from my wrist during a walk and the audio quality held up.
 The square form factor and lightweight build make it one of the most comfortable smartwatches I tested for all-day wear, including sleep. Sleep Profile gave me a weekly breakdown of my sleep stages with comparisons to my baselines, which is more useful than a single Sleep Score. Stress Management Score, SpO2, and mindfulness content round out the women’s-health suite.
 Daily Readiness Score and Active Zone Minutes motivate activity, while the workout intensity map after a GPS-tracked run shows heart rate zones along your route. Built-in GPS is accurate on open routes but drifts in dense tree cover or urban canyons.  The Google Pay migration from Fitbit Pay broke some AmEx cards, which is the most common complaint in Amazon reviews. There’s no music control or camera control, so iPhone users will miss features they take for granted. Sleep and heart rate tracking can be unreliable during wet conditions, like swimming or sweaty HIIT sessions. Auto exercise detection sometimes interrupts during breaks and asks if you want to stop the workout.
 Fitbit Versa 4: who it’s best for
 The Versa 4 is the best fitness tracker for women who want a true smartwatch experience with a bright AMOLED, Bluetooth calling, and Fitbit’s health suite at a mid-tier price.  The Garmin Venu 3 is the premium pick in this roundup, and after 5 weeks of daily wear I can confirm it earns the price tag for the right buyer. The 14-day battery life is the standout — I went on a 10-day camping trip without packing the charger and came back with 30% to spare. The 1.8-inch AMOLED is the largest in Garmin’s fitness-tracker line, and at 1.6 ounces it’s lighter than it looks.
 For women who want one watch for everything, the Venu 3 delivers: Body Battery, sleep coaching with HRV status, 30+ built-in sports apps, on-wrist phone calls, and a voice assistant that lets you reply to texts from your wrist. The training features include workout benefit (did this session improve my fitness?), recovery time, and Garmin Coach adaptive plans for 5K, 10K, and half marathon goals.
 Build quality is excellent — the stainless steel bezel and AMOLED display feel premium. Sleep tracking is consistent with the Garmin ecosystem standard: HRV status, sleep stages, and personalized coaching. Heart rate accuracy on chest-strap comparison runs held within 1-2 bpm.  The trade-off is the price. At more than double the cost of the Vivoactive 5, you pay for the larger display, longer battery, and added microphone. The third-party app catalog remains Garmin’s weak spot — if you live in the Apple or Google app ecosystems, you’ll miss the depth of those integrations.
 Garmin Venu 3: who it’s best for
 The Venu 3 is the best fitness tracker for women who want a premium smartwatch with Garmin’s health ecosystem, long battery life, and on-wrist voice replies. It’s ideal for serious athletes, busy executives, and anyone who wants one watch that handles everything from a board meeting to a marathon.

 The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most natural choice for iPhone owners, and after 4 weeks of testing I can confirm it delivers premium smartwatch features at a more accessible price than the flagship Apple Watch. The Vitals app and sleep apnea notifications are genuinely useful — sleep apnea detection alone has caught undiagnosed cases in multiple Amazon reviewers who then sought medical care.
 Workout Buddy powered by Apple Intelligence is a fun addition that gives you real-time coaching motivation during runs and walks. The wrist temperature sensor adds data to the cycle-tracking experience, which is more accurate than calendar-only predictions. Fall detection and crash detection auto-connect to emergency services if you’re unresponsive — a meaningful safety feature for solo runners, hikers, and older women living alone.
 The always-on display makes a real difference for daily use — you can glance at the time and notifications without raising your wrist. Bluetooth calling, texts, music, podcasts, and Siri integration are seamless on iPhone. The 2x faster charging (8 hours of battery in 15 minutes) is the most underrated upgrade — I could shower, dress, and head out the door with enough battery for the day.
 The daily charging requirement is the trade-off. If you want to wear it for sleep tracking, you need to charge during your morning routine, which is doable but adds a habit to manage. The 40mm size fits smaller wrists well, but the default band may not work for everyone — most users swap in a third-party band. Wheelchair mode step tracking can be inaccurate for some users.
 Apple Watch SE 3: who it’s best for
 The SE 3 is the best fitness tracker for women who live in the Apple ecosystem and want seamless iPhone integration, sleep apnea detection, and crash/fall safety features. It’s ideal for iPhone owners, older women who want emergency detection, and anyone who values the Apple Health app’s depth.
 Skip it if you want multi-day battery life, want to avoid daily charging, or use an Android phone. For Android users, the Fitbit Versa 4 or Garmin Vivoactive 5 are stronger picks.

 Runners who need pace and distance on the watch, women trying to conceive who need skin-temperature-based ovulation tracking, or buyers wanting premium build quality should look at higher-tier options.
 Check Latest Price on Amazon 
 Affiliate link 
 How to Choose the Best Fitness Tracker for Women
 Choosing the best fitness tracker for women comes down to matching the device to your body, your cycle, and your lifestyle. Below is the framework our team uses when readers ask which one to buy.
 Cycle, Fertility, and Pregnancy Tracking
 The single biggest difference between women’s-specific and generic trackers is reproductive-health features. The Fitbit Inspire 3, Fitbit Charge 6, Fitbit Versa 4, Apple Watch SE 3, and Garmin Vivoactive 6 all offer menstrual cycle tracking with skin temperature-based fertile window prediction. If you’re trying to conceive, prioritize skin-temperature data over calendar-only logging — calendar predictions assume a 28-day cycle and miss women with irregular periods.
 Perimenopause and menopause tracking is rare in the fitness tracker category, but the Garmin Vivoactive 5 and Vivoactive 6 track HRV status, sleep quality, and cycle irregularity — all key signals during the menopause transition. Pregnancy tracking modes are built into Garmin Connect, Apple Watch, and Fitbit, with weekly fetal development updates and weight tracking. Our budget fitness tracker roundup covers options that include basic cycle tracking.
 Battery Life That Lasts
 Battery life separates fitness bands from full smartwatches. The Fitbit Inspire 3 averages 10 days, the Garmin Vivoactive 5 and 6 average 11 days, and the Garmin Venu 3 stretches to 14 days. Apple Watch SE 3 requires daily charging if you wear it for sleep tracking, which is a meaningful trade-off. If you hate daily charging, Garmin and Fitbit trackers win on longevity.
 GPS mode drains battery fastest. The Garmin Forerunner 165 lasts 19 hours in GPS mode, which is enough for a marathon plus warm-up and cool-down. If you run regularly with GPS, factor that into your battery budget.
 Fit and Comfort on Small Wrists
 Most roundups skip this, but it’s the single most common complaint on Reddit’s r/PetiteFitness and r/FitnessTrackers. The Fitbit Inspire 3 is the slimmest option at 0.76 inches wide and 3.8 ounces. The Garmin Forerunner 165 and Vivoactive 5 are the smallest Garmin cases at 42-43mm, designed for smaller wrists. The Garmin Venu 3 at 45mm and Apple Watch SE 3 at 40mm fit most women but feel bulky on a 4.75-inch wrist circumference.
 Band width matters as much as case size. The Fitbit Inspire 3, Garmin Vivoactive 5, and Garmin Forerunner 165 use 20mm bands, which are easier to size down for petite wrists than the wider bands on the Fitbit Versa 4 or Fitbit Charge 6. Our related guide on fitness trackers for weightlifting covers durability for high-impact wear.
 Smartwatch vs Dedicated Tracker
 Dedicated trackers (Fitbit Inspire 3, Garmin Vivosmart 5) are slimmer, lighter, and last longer on a charge but lack apps and on-wrist replies. Smartwatches (Apple Watch SE 3, Fitbit Versa 4, Garmin Venu 3) deliver apps, calls, and music controls but require more frequent charging and have larger cases. If you want one device that replaces your watch, go smartwatch. If you want a sleep-friendly tracker you forget you’re wearing, go dedicated.
 Subscription Cost
 Subscription fatigue is a real pain point. Garmin Connect is free for all features. Fitbit Premium costs extra per month and unlocks advanced insights like Sleep Profile details and Daily Readiness historical trends. Oura requires a subscription. WHOOP is subscription-only with no device purchase. If subscription cost matters, Garmin trackers and the Fitbit Inspire 3 (without Premium) are the strongest no-subscription choices.
 Ecosystem Compatibility
 iPhone users get the deepest experience with Apple Watch SE 3. Android users get the deepest Google integration with Fitbit Charge 6 and Fitbit Versa 4. Garmin works well on both platforms, which is why it’s our most-recommended cross-platform brand. Check your phone model compatibility before buying — the Fitbit Charge 6 requires Android 11+ and iOS 16.4+, while the Fitpolo works back to iOS 10 and Android 5.
 Ring vs Wrist-Worn: A Quick Comparison
 Oura Ring is the most popular ring-style tracker, but it’s not in this roundup because it’s a different form factor. Rings win on comfort during sleep and don’t look like fitness gear. They lose on real-time glanceability, on-wrist calls, and built-in GPS. If you want a tracker you wear 24/7 and never think about, a ring is appealing. If you want glanceable data, on-wrist replies, and workout-focused metrics, stick with a wrist tracker. Our under-300 roundup covers budget wrist options.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best fitness tracker for women?
 The best fitness tracker for women is the Fitbit Inspire 3 thanks to its slim 0.76-inch case, 10-day battery, built-in menstrual cycle tracking, and 4.2-star rating across more than 25,000 reviews. It fits comfortably on small wrists, tracks heart rate and sleep automatically, and works with both iPhone and Android. For runners, the Garmin Forerunner 165 is a stronger pick thanks to its built-in GPS and 11-day battery. For iPhone users wanting the deepest ecosystem integration, the Apple Watch SE 3 is the top choice.
 What is the best fitness tracker for women with small wrists?
 The Fitbit Inspire 3 is the best fitness tracker for women with small wrists thanks to its 0.76-inch case width, lightweight 3.8-ounce build, and narrow silicone band that fits wrists as small as 4.75 inches. The Garmin Vivoactive 5 and Forerunner 165 are the next-best petite-fit Garmin options at 42-43mm cases. The Garmin Lily 2 Active is another jewelry-inspired option for very small wrists, though we did not test it in this roundup. Avoid the Garmin Venu 3 (45mm) and Apple Watch SE 3 (40mm) if your wrist is under 5.5 inches — the cases will feel bulky.
 Can a smartwatch track my menstrual cycle?
 Yes, most modern smartwatches can track your menstrual cycle, though the depth varies. The Fitbit Inspire 3, Fitbit Charge 6, Fitbit Versa 4, Apple Watch SE 3, and Garmin Vivoactive 6 all offer menstrual cycle tracking with skin temperature-based fertile window prediction. The Apple Watch SE 3 uses wrist temperature sensing for added accuracy. Calendar-only logging is less accurate for women with irregular cycles. For perimenopause and menopause tracking, the Garmin Vivoactive 5 and Vivoactive 6 track HRV status and sleep quality changes that signal hormonal shifts.
 Is Garmin Lily 2 worth it?
 The Garmin Lily 2 is worth it for women who want a jewelry-inspired fitness tracker with a small case and pattern lens design. It tracks steps, sleep, heart rate, stress, and menstrual cycle with Garmin’s free Connect app. The trade-offs are a grayscale display that’s harder to read in sunlight, no built-in GPS, and no on-wrist replies to texts. If those limitations don’t bother you and you prioritize style and comfort over advanced metrics, the Lily 2 is a solid choice. For more advanced training metrics, the Garmin Vivoactive 5 or Forerunner 165 deliver more depth.
 Which is more reliable, Garmin or Fitbit?
 Both Garmin and Fitbit are reliable fitness tracker brands, but they serve different priorities. Garmin wins on battery life, sensor accuracy for serious athletes, and no-mandatory-subscription policies. Fitbit wins on a more intuitive app, deeper Google services integration (Maps, Wallet, YouTube Music), and a friendlier onboarding experience for beginners. For women prioritizing reproductive-health tracking, both brands offer menstrual cycle tracking with skin temperature data. For women wanting adaptive training plans and longer battery life, Garmin is the stronger pick. For casual users wanting simplicity and Google integration, Fitbit is the better fit.
 Our Final Verdict on the Best Fitness Trackers for Women
 After three months of daily wear across 10 devices, our team’s pick for the best fitness tracker for women in 2026 remains the Fitbit Inspire 3. It nails the three filters that actually matter for women’s trackers: a slim case that fits petite wrists, built-in menstrual cycle tracking with skin temperature data, and a 10-day battery that doesn’t require daily charging.
 If you’re a runner, choose the Garmin Forerunner 165 for built-in GPS and adaptive training plans. If you’re on a budget, the Gydom Smart Watch delivers more features than its price suggests. If you live in the Apple ecosystem, the Apple Watch SE 3 is the natural pick. And if you want Garmin’s newest health-tracking features with smart wake alarm and animated workouts, the Garmin Vivoactive 6 is worth the premium.
 Whatever you choose, prioritize the device that fits your wrist, tracks your cycle, and matches your lifestyle — not the one with the most features on the spec sheet. Your tracker should disappear on your wrist, not remind you that you’re wearing tech.

 Last updated: October 30, 2026 · Based on manufacturer specifications, independent expert reviews and verified user feedback — see our Research Process .
 If you have small or narrow wrists, the best smartwatch is usually one with a small case (roughly 35–42mm), a low profile that doesn’t tip over the wrist bone, and a lightweight build . Based on manufacturer specifications and published expert and user reviews, the standout options are the Garmin Lily 2 (the smallest mainstream pick at 35.4mm), the Apple Watch SE (40mm) for iPhone owners, compact Android choices like the Samsung Galaxy Watch (40mm) and Google Pixel Watch 3 (41mm) , and the slim hybrid Withings ScanWatch Light (37mm) . This guide explains how to judge fit and matches each pick to a type of buyer.
 Smartwatch Trends is reader-supported. When you buy through links on our site we may earn an affiliate commission, at no extra cost to you. As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases.
 Quick answer
 For most small wrists, the Garmin Lily 2 (35.4mm) is the easiest fit, while the 40mm Apple Watch SE and 40mm Samsung Galaxy Watch are the best small-case options for iPhone and Android users.
 Our picks at a glance
 Each pick is explained in full further down.

 Key takeaways
 Case diameter, thickness and weight matter more than screen specs for a small-wrist fit
 A 40–42mm case suits most narrow wrists; sub-36mm models like the Lily 2 fit the smallest
 Band length and lug-to-lug span decide whether a watch actually sits flat, so check both before buying
 Index 
 How we picked
 Smartwatch Trends is an independent, research-based resource. We do not run a testing lab, so this guide is built from official manufacturer specifications (case diameter, thickness, weight and band sizing) combined with published expert reviews and aggregated user feedback about comfort and fit. We prioritized watches with:
 A small case diameter — generally 35–42mm, since larger cases overhang narrow wrists.
 A modest thickness and weight , so the watch doesn’t feel top-heavy or catch on sleeves.
 Short-enough band options , including small/compact straps or extra holes, so the watch can be cinched snugly.
 Reliable core health and fitness features , so a smaller size doesn’t mean giving up essentials like heart rate, GPS and sleep tracking.
 We did not assign numeric scores or star ratings. Where fit is subjective, we say so—wrist shape varies, and the only true test is trying a watch on or measuring your wrist first.
 Tip: Measure your wrist with a soft tape or a strip of paper before buying. Most narrow wrists fall between 130–160mm in circumference; many bands list their fit range in millimeters, which makes matching easier. 
 What “small wrist” really means for fit
 Screen size and processor get the headlines, but three physical specs decide whether a watch looks and feels right on a small wrist:
 Case diameter — the width of the watch body. Anything much above 44mm tends to overhang a narrow wrist visually.
 Lug-to-lug / footprint — how far the case and band attachment points span top to bottom. A short footprint lets the watch sit flat instead of see-sawing.
 Thickness and weight — a thinner, lighter watch is less likely to feel bulky or spin around the wrist.
 Band length matters too. A great case ruined by a strap that won’t cinch tight is a common complaint, so look for models that ship with a small/compact band or sell one separately.
 The best smartwatches for small wrists
 1. Garmin Lily 2 — best for the smallest wrists
 At about 35.4mm and roughly 24–25g (without strap), the Lily 2 is the most petite mainstream smartwatch here. Garmin designed it explicitly with smaller wrists and a fashion-forward look in mind, with a patterned lens that hides the display until it lights up.
 Why it fits: Its sub-36mm case and light weight make it one of the few watches that won’t overhang very narrow wrists. Who it’s for: Buyers who want an elegant, discreet wearable with solid step, sleep and heart-rate tracking and multi-day battery life, and who don’t need onboard GPS or a large app ecosystem.
 Check price › 
 2. Apple Watch SE (40mm) — best value for iPhone users
 The 40mm Apple Watch SE pairs a compact case with the core Apple Watch experience—heart-rate alerts, fall and crash detection, fitness tracking and tight iPhone integration—at a lower price than the flagship line.
 Why it fits: The 40mm size and short/small-fit Apple bands suit narrow wrists, and Apple sells multiple band lengths. Who it’s for: iPhone owners who want a small, capable watch without paying for the always-on display or ECG of the pricier models. New to the platform? See our walkthrough on how to set up an Apple Watch for the first time .
 Check price › 
 3. Apple Watch Series (42mm) — best overall for iPhone
 The current flagship Series uses a 42mm case (alongside a larger 46mm option) with slimmer borders and a thin profile, so the footprint stays reasonable for many small wrists despite the bigger screen.
 Why it fits: A thin case and large, easy-to-read display in a still-compact body, plus advanced health features like ECG and an always-on screen. Who it’s for: iPhone users who want the fullest feature set in the smallest available flagship size. If you’re curious how its ECG works, read what a smartwatch ECG actually measures .
 4. Samsung Galaxy Watch (40mm) — best for Android and Samsung phones
 Samsung’s Galaxy Watch line offers a 40mm case alongside the larger 44mm. The smaller size keeps the round body manageable on narrow wrists while retaining Wear OS apps, GPS and a full health suite.
 Why it fits: A true 40mm round case with swappable standard bands, so finding a short strap is easy. Who it’s for: Android users—especially Samsung phone owners—who want a compact round watch with rich tracking and a deep app ecosystem.
 5. Google Pixel Watch 3 (41mm) — best compact design for Android
 The Pixel Watch 3’s 41mm version has a domed glass design that minimizes the visible footprint, and it leans on Fitbit’s health platform for sleep, heart rate and activity tracking.
 Why it fits: The rounded, edge-to-edge design makes a 41mm case look and feel smaller than the number suggests. Who it’s for: Android users who want a clean, modern look with strong Fitbit-based wellness tracking and Google services.
 Check price › 
 6. Withings ScanWatch Light (37mm) — best low-profile hybrid
 If a chunky touchscreen isn’t for you, the ScanWatch Light is a 37mm hybrid that looks like a traditional analog watch, with a small sub-dial and a tiny display for essentials. It emphasizes long battery life and discreet health tracking.
 Why it fits: A slim, light analog-style case that disappears on a small wrist. Who it’s for: Buyers who prioritize style, weeks-long battery life and basic wellness metrics over apps and notifications.
 Quick comparison

 iPhone vs Android: which small watch?

 Pairs only with iPhone

 Your phone usually decides the platform: Apple Watches work only with iPhone, while Samsung, Google and Garmin models support Android (and several support iPhone too). Once platform is set, choose the smallest case that still shows the features you care about.
 Don’t overlook these factors
 Battery life: Smaller cases often mean smaller batteries. If endurance matters, compare models in our guide to which smartwatch lasts the longest .
 Water resistance: If you swim or shower with your watch, check the rating—see how water-resistance ratings work .
 Band swaps: A snug fit is half the battle. Replacing the stock band with a shorter or sport loop style can transform comfort on a narrow wrist.
 Important: Smartwatch health features—heart rate, ECG, SpO2 and sleep stages—are wellness tools, not medical devices. A poor fit on a small wrist can reduce sensor accuracy. Don't use readings to diagnose or treat any condition; consult a clinician for medical concerns. 
 Who should buy
 For the smallest wrists or a fashion-first look, the Garmin Lily 2 is the easiest fit. iPhone owners are best served by the Apple Watch SE (40mm) for value or the 42mm Series for full features. Android users should look at the Samsung Galaxy Watch (40mm) or Pixel Watch 3 (41mm) . Whatever you choose, confirm the case diameter and band fit range against your wrist measurement before ordering.
 Where to buy

 As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases. Prices and availability are accurate as of the time of purchase.
 Frequently asked questions
 What case size is best for a small wrist?
 For most narrow wrists, a 40–42mm case fits well, while sub-36mm models like the Garmin Lily 2 (35.4mm) suit the smallest wrists. Beyond diameter, check the watch’s thickness and lug-to-lug footprint so it sits flat without overhanging.
 Do smaller smartwatches have worse battery life?
 Often, yes—smaller cases tend to house smaller batteries, so a compact watch may need more frequent charging than a large one. Hybrid models like the Withings ScanWatch Light are an exception, trading a full touchscreen for much longer runtime. See our battery-life comparison for details.
 Does a smaller watch affect heart-rate or sleep accuracy?
 Sensor accuracy depends more on a snug, consistent fit than on case size. A watch that’s too loose—common when a band can’t cinch small enough—can produce less reliable optical heart-rate and sleep-stage readings . Choosing a properly sized band helps regardless of model.
 Can I make a larger smartwatch fit a small wrist?
 To a point. Swapping in a shorter or sport-loop band improves comfort, but it can’t shrink the case—an oversized body will still overhang a narrow wrist visually and may rock when you move. Starting with a smaller case is the better approach.

Smartwatches for small wrists: the models that fit 
 Smartwatches for small wrists, by the numbers
 A small wrist kills smartwatches two ways: the case overhangs the wrist edges, and the band bottoms out at its smallest setting before it is snug [4] [7] . Both failures are checkable before you buy, with numbers the manufacturers publish. This page lists the models that actually fit small wrists with their case dimensions, weights, and official band minimums, and the two checks that decide fit. It is the model-picking companion to our step-by-step smartwatch sizing guide and the full smartwatch case-size table .
 Three things to know before shopping. 
 The band minimum, not the case size, decides fit on small wrists: Garmin's Lily 2 fits from 110mm, Apple's S/M bands from 130mm, Versa 4 small bands from 130mm [1] [5] [6] .
 The smallest true smartwatches are genuinely small: Lily 2 is 35.4 x 35.4 x 10.1mm and 24g [1] [2] .
 Under 150mm circumference, skip 44mm-class cases entirely; 42mm+ overhangs and the bands often start at 140mm or higher [4] [7] .
 The small-wrist smartwatch table
 Manufacturer-published dimensions and wrist-fit figures, each cross-checked against at least two sources:
 Model Case (mm) Weight Official wrist fit Band width 
 Garmin Lily 2 / Classic 35.4 x 35.4 x 10.1 24g 110-175mm 14mm 
 Garmin Lily 2 Active 38 x 38 x 11 28g 110-175mm class 14mm 
 Apple Watch SE / Series, 40mm class ~40 x 36 x 10.7 ~27-31g S/M band from 130mm proprietary 
 Samsung Galaxy Watch, 40mm 40.4 x 40.4 x 9.7 (Watch7) ~28-31g S/M band ~130-190mm 20mm 
 Fitbit Versa 4 family, small band 40.5 x 40.5 x 11.2 ~38g with band S band 130-178mm proprietary 
 Fitbit Luxe (tracker) slim steel tracker ~34g S band 140-180mm proprietary 
 Fitbit Inspire 3 (tracker) 39.3 x 18.6 x 11.75 body 17.7g S band 130-190mm proprietary 
 Sources: Garmin Lily 2 dimensions and 110-175mm wrist range from Garmin's published specs as transcribed by fitness-tracker-test.info and recoveryforathletes.com [1] [2] ; Apple and Galaxy band ranges from the manufacturer tables on our Apple band size and smartwatch sizing pages, cross-checked against MacRumors' band guide [5] ; numbered Apple loop sizes on our Solo Loop sizing chart ; Versa 4 small-band 130-178mm from Fitbit's official chart on our Versa band page [6] ; Luxe 140-180mm and Inspire 3 130-190mm small-band figures from the Fitbit Luxe manual (140-180mm S band) and Google Store's Inspire 3 spec page (130-190mm small) [3] [8] . Inspire 3 body is 39.32 x 18.6 x 11.75mm per Google Store [8] .
 Why the Lily 2 is the floor
 Garmin built the Lily line for exactly this problem: a 35.4mm case (38mm on the Active version with built-in GPS), 10.1mm thick, 24g with strap, on 14mm quick-release bands, fitting wrists from 110mm circumference [1] [2] . Nothing else that runs a real app ecosystem goes lower. The trade-offs are honest: a monochrome patterned-lens display, connected GPS only on the base model, and no ECG; the Lily 2 Active adds GPS and buttons in the larger 38mm case at 28g [2] . Band ecosystem note: the 14mm lug width is narrower than Garmin's QuickFit standard elsewhere, so check our Garmin band size page before buying spares.
 The two checks before you buy any smartwatch
 Check 1: the band minimum. Find the manufacturer's "fits wrists" figure for the band that ships with the case you chose. Apple publishes S/M and M/L ranges per band type (S/M roughly 130-180mm) [5] ; Samsung quotes S/M and M/L bands around 130-190 and 145-205mm rather than per-case figures [6] ; Fitbit prints S/L ranges on the box (Versa 4 small: 130-178mm) [6] . If your wrist is below the small band's floor, the watch will never be snug, and a loose smartwatch is not just uncomfortable: gaps under the sensor degrade heart-rate accuracy [4] .
 Check 2: overhang. Case width plus lugs must not exceed your wrist width, the flat top of your wrist. Measure your wrist circumference (60 seconds, no tools, on our how to measure page), convert to wrist width with the calculator , and compare against the case's longer dimension. Round 40mm cases are 40.4mm wide (Galaxy Watch7) [6] ; squarish Apple cases run about 40 x 36mm, which is why they wear smaller than the number suggests. The full method, with the mistake list, is in our sizing guide's overhang check .
 What to skip on a small wrist
 44mm and 46mm cases (Galaxy Watch 44, Apple 44/46mm, Venu 3 45mm): overhang plus bands that often start at 145mm [6] [7] .
 Ultra-class 49mm watches: 130-210mm band range aside, the case is a brick on a sub-150mm wrist [6] .
 "One size" bands with no published minimum: if the maker will not print the floor, assume it is too high [7] .
 If the watch you want is borderline, the band can be fixed after the fact (smaller aftermarket bands, or the elastic and nylon options on our materials page ), but the case cannot. When both sizes of a model exist, this page's numbers plus the calculator decide: see how to choose between the two sizes .

by
Conor Allison
◆
August 4, 2026 10AM

15 min read
There are plenty of wearables without a huge screen that can track your health and wellness accurately

Tracking fitness and health doesn’t have to involve wearing a big screen on your wrist. With the rise of smart rings and screenless fitness trackers, you can now discreetly and accurately monitor your health and activity around the clock.

Some may be put off by the bright displays on modern smartwatches, while others may not be able to wear a watch for practical reasons. Whatever the case, there are excellent screen-free alternatives.

In 2026, most major brands offer solid options—Hume Health, WHOOP, Garmin, Oura, and Amazfit all make discreet wearables designed for continuous health and fitness tracking. And here at Wareable, we've tested them all.

So, in this guide to the best screenless fitness trackers and discreet wearables, we've compiled our top recommendations from in-depth reviews to help you find the right device for your needs.

At a glance: Best screenless fitness trackers
Hume Band 2.0: Best screenless fitness tracker overall
RingConn Gen 2: Best for battery life and comfort
Oura Ring 4: Best smart ring for health tracking
WHOOP 5.0: Best screenless tracker for recovery and training
Ultrahuman Ring Air: Best subscription-free smart ring
What to consider when choosing a screenless fitness tracker
(Image credit: Wareable)
Which type of discreet fitness tracker should you choose?

Screenless fitness trackers generally fall into four categories, each with different strengths and trade-offs:

Screenless bands: e.g., WHOOP, Hume Band 2.0, Amazfit Helio Strap. These are fabric bands with a sensor pod. They are well-suited for 24/7 data collection and can often be worn on the biceps for improved heart rate accuracy during workouts. They are ‘data-first’ devices.
Smart rings: e.g., Oura, RingConn, Ultrahuman. The most subtle option. These are brilliant for passive 24/7 tracking, especially sleep and temperature. However, they’re not great for workouts (due to potential scratching and less reliable HR readings).
Hybrid watches: e.g., Withings, Garmin Lily. These look like traditional analog watches but have hidden displays and sensors. This is the ‘hidden in plain sight’ option, perfect for the office.
Clip-on/pendant trackers: e.g., Fitbit Inspire, Xiaomi Smart Band. These are the most versatile, as the sensor pod can be removed from a strap and placed in a clip or necklace.
The heart rate data trade-off

This is the most important compromise. If you wear a tracker as a pendant or clip-on (like the Xiaomi or Fitbit options), it is no longer in contact with your skin.

This means you will lose all advanced tracking. You will not get heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), stress, SpO2, or advanced sleep stage data. It will essentially become a very simple step counter.

Battery life and the subscription model

By forgoing a power-intensive AMOLED display, most devices on our list have excellent battery life, ranging from five days to a full month.

However, be aware of the cost model. Premium trackers like WHOOP and Oura require a mandatory monthly subscription to access your data and insights.

As a result, subscription-free alternatives like Amazfit Helio Strap and Ultrahuman Ring Air are becoming increasingly popular.

Screenless trackers expected in 2026: Garmin and more
(Image credit: Wareable)

We expect the trend of screenless wearables to continue to gain momentum in 2026, with credible leaks and reports suggesting that major brands are preparing all-new discreet devices for launch.

In fact, we’ve already seen our first concrete suggestions that Garmin is preparing its long-awaited WHOOP rival for release.

In January, a Garmin CIRQA listing accidentally appeared on several of the brand’s official websites. Although no full images of the device were shown, its description as a Smart Band—and the placeholder regarding shipping timeframes—suggested it may launch in late spring or early summer, but no official announcements have been made yet.

Following WHOOP’s early victory in its legal quest to block rival Lexqi from sale in the US, we also expect further litigation regarding competitors’ screenless wristband designs.

Hume Band
(Image credit: Wareable)

Try Hume Band 2.0 Now

Hume Band 2.0 in brief:
Screenless wellness tracker
Latest discreet wearable release
Has metabolic, recovery, and blood pressure trend tracking
Available in one color

After testing, we think Hume Band 2.0 sits between WHOOP 5.0 and Oura Ring 4, but this brand uses a different approach. It’s a screenless wristband designed to track what’s happening inside your body rather than what you do on the surface.

You’ll get the same biometrics as the original Hume Band like heart rate, HRV, SpO₂, using five LEDs and four photodiodes. Yet, blood pressure trend tracking sets it apart—it analyzes patterns over time to deepen insights and offers tips for your well-being. Also, Hume Health has upcoming features planned for later in the year.

The latest model brings some solid improvements: new strap material, color, and a significantly better battery life. That said, because the sensors haven’t changed, we found step tracking accuracy quite off. So think of the 2.0 as a well-being companion rather than a performance-focused tracker.

Here’s what really stands out: battery life jumped up to 14 days on a single charge. With screenless wearables, battery is what truly matters. No AMOLED screen means longer battery life, so you can go weeks without thinking about the device.

As for the design, you’re getting UltraLux material in a light, subtle gray color. It’s breathable, adjustable, water-resistant, and the new shade makes it easier to hide under your sleeves while keeping the sensors snug against your skin for around-the-clock tracking.

Great battery life
Easy to incorporate color
New features coming later
CONS:
Step tracking isn’t accurate
Limited to one color option
RingConn Gen 2
(Image credit: Wareable)

RingConn Gen 2 Air

Details
RingConn Gen 2 in brief:
Subscription-free Oura alternative
Slim, lightweight design
Tracks heart rate, HRV, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and sleep stages
The battery can survive up to 12 days on a single charge

If you’re disappointed that Oura Ring 4’s new design is still chunky, RingConn definitely goes in a very different direction. It’s lighter and feels more like a ring on the finger than a gadget.

What surprised us most is that, unlike most trackers, it has a sleep apnea tracker. RingConn’s algorithms use breathing patterns, oxygen levels, HRV, and movement to flag irregularities that may be associated with overnight breathing disruptions.

We don’t recommend using it for clinical diagnosis or as a medical device, but it may be a useful early indicator for those who suspect sleep-related breathing issues.

Besides that, it stands out with its battery life. A single charge lasts up to 12 days, which is really impressive compared to Oura Ring 4.

We’re not saying you should switch from Oura Ring 4 to RingConn Gen 2. Both have advantages and disadvantages; you just need to choose your preference. However, RingConn Gen 2 is a better substitute if you’re not willing to splurge.

PROS:
Offers a free sizing kit
Tracks stress levels through a dedicated stress index
Has lifetime access to all personal data
CONS:
No charging plug included in the box
Could improve global accessibility and setup convenience
Oura Ring 4
(Image credit: Wareable)

Try Oura Ring 4 Now

Oura Ring 4 in brief:
Ensures hidden tracking, though it is relatively chunky
Provides in-depth insights into stress, heart, steps, sleep, and more
Automatic workout tracking—but not the best form factor for tracking exercise
Up to 8 days of battery life
Requires a monthly subscription fee

Smart rings have proven to be the most subtle wearable tech form factor over the last few years, and Oura Ring 4 is one of the best you can buy right now.

We were a little disappointed that Oura didn’t slim down the design further in Ring 4, but it is now more accurate, with more sensors that lead to virtually no gaps in tracking data. Oura also touts improved workout tracking accuracy for Ring 4.

Yet, while we loved the longitudinal insights into our cardio health, this still isn’t a tracker we recommend for workouts. Instead, Oura Ring 4 excels as a holistic tracker. It delivers exceptional insights into stress-associated triggers and resilience, engaging daily scores based on a wide range of biomarkers, and offers plenty of partnerships in health and fitness to flesh out its own data.

The sleep tracking is also particularly impressive, with data we grade as the best you can find on any wearable. It’s also much less obstructive to wear at night than a wrist gadget.

Like WHOOP 5.0/MG, the biggest downside is the price, as you’ll need to pay for an expensive ring and commit to a subscription. Still, this is an excellent option if you want robust wellness metrics without using a wrist fitness tracker.

PROS:
One of the best wellness trackers out there
Smart circadian insights
Brilliant presentation of data
CONS:
Rivals are thinner and more comfortable
Really expensive
Workout tracking is still iffy
WHOOP 5.0/MG
(Image credit: Wareable)

Try WHOOP 5.0/MG Now

WHOOP 5.0 in brief:
Tacks stress, heart rate, respiratory rate, HRV, blood oxygen, and temperature
Requires a pricey subscription model
Best for data-driven athletes focused on recovery

Discreet wearables tend to be light on metrics, but the opposite is true with WHOOP 5.0.

The 2025 release is one of the most advanced options on our list, collecting serious health stats like Healthspan and insights focused on recovery, strain, sleep, and stress.

The WHOOP subscription plan you choose when buying or upgrading dictates which device you get—5.0 or MG—and the latter can unlock ECG and blood pressure estimates.

Post-testing comparison: WHOOP MG vs. 5.0

WHOOP’s screenless design makes it significantly more discreet than most when worn on the wrist, and WHOOP Body clothing (which hides the tracker in garments) means its versatility is unmatched. This has been expanded for the 5.0 generation to include bralettes, vests, and more, though neither the 5.0 nor MG designs will work with bands designed for 4.0—a real shame.

The recovery master—but for a price

We’ve worn WHOOP daily as part of ongoing testing against other trackers over the past few years. The core wellness metrics, Stress Monitor and Health Monitor, are excellent and intuitive, and compare well in terms of accuracy with industry-leading wearables. As part of the 5.0 update, even the basics, such as step tracking, have been refined.

However, our main criticisms of WHOOP remain its inconsistent HR readings during workouts and its high price. It works via a subscription rather than a one-and-done payment, making it one of the most expensive long-term wearables to invest in.

However, there’s nothing else quite like it, which is why it’s such a good fit for many.

Check out our full WHOOP 5.0 review
PROS:
Vast and useful new health and wellness features
Battery life upgrade is game-changing
Pricing tiers and device choice are improved
CONS:
HR accuracy still isn’t elite
WHOOP 4.0 bands aren’t compatible
Subscription-only model won’t be for everyone
Ultrahuman Ring Air
(Image credit: Wareable)

Try Ultrahuman Ring Air Now

Ultrahuman Ring Air in brief
Lightweight titanium ring focuses on sleep, circadian rhythm, and overall wellness
Tracks sleep, recovery, HRV, resting heart rate, skin temperature, and activity
Provides limited workout tracking; heart rate data not ideal for exercise
Battery life is around five days

If Oura Ring piqued your interest but its ongoing subscription cost made you pause, consider Ultrahuman Ring Air.

This is a lightweight and comfortable smart ring, weighing only 2.4g. The feature set is very similar to Oura’s. Sleep is the primary focus, and a Sleep Index considers a wide range of data and metrics. We found the sleep tracking largely reliable, with accuracy comparable to its smart ring rival and WHOOP.

It also focuses on recovery and helps manage circadian rhythms, including regulating stimulants and encouraging healthy wind-down times. Priced at $349.00 without ongoing subscriptions, it presents a cost-effective alternative.

However, be cautious: like all smart rings, it’s not a great device for tracking active workouts, as it’s prone to scratches and HR inaccuracy during exercise.

PROS:
Solid health data
Stimulant window data is interesting
Thoughtful prompts and recommendations
CONS:
Circadian window needs to be developed
Still chunky
Lack of breathing rate data

Withings ScanWatch 2
(Image credit: Wareable)

Try Withings ScanWatch 2 Now

Withings ScanWatch 2 in brief:
Classic-styled hybrid watch with a grayscale display dial
Tracks heart rate, ECG, SpO2, sleep, activity, and temperature trends
Provides improved heart rate accuracy from the original ScanWatch
No built-in GPS for outdoor exercise
Up to 35 days of battery life

Withings ScanWatch 2 is the best hybrid for deep health tracking—and an update last year makes it an even more compelling pick. The changes haven’t affected the look; this is still a premium analog watch with a small monochrome screen for stats and notifications.

Instead, it now offers an exceptional 35 days between charges (up from 30 on older versions of the ScanWatch 2) and can power Withings’ AI-driven HealthSense 4 OS. This updated software crunches data from 35 biomarkers to power a new Vitality Indicator that aims to give you a clearer picture of how fatigued you may be and why.

It also introduces predictive health alerts that may notify you of changes that could be associated with illness or the start of your menstrual cycle. Add all that to the existing features—ECG for identifying potential signs of AFib and SpO2 monitoring for tracking possible breathing disturbances during sleep—and it becomes a fairly formidable package.

So, for those who want robust, discreet health monitoring without sacrificing style, this is the top choice.

Check out our full Withings ScanWatch 2 review
PROS:
Solid and sleek design
Top battery life
Breathing and temp data
CONS:
Insights slightly lagging rivals
Sleep data is not the best in class
Rogue workout detection
Amazfit Helio Strap
(Image credit: Wareable)

Try Amazfit Helio Strap

Amazfit Helio Strap in brief:
No subscription
Can be worn on the wrist or (optional) arm strap
Offers accurate heart rate tracking when worn on the upper arm
Best as a powerful, low-cost, subscription-free alternative to WHOOP

Amazfit Helio Strap delivers on its promise as a compelling, subscription-free alternative to WHOOP.

The hardware is lightweight (just 20g), comfortable, and has a 10-day battery life. Its core heart rate and sleep tracking are impressively accurate—particularly when the sensor is worn on the optional upper-arm strap.

In our testing, the arm-worn sensor was nearly identical to a Garmin chest strap (within 1–2BPM), making it a reliable training tool.

The tracker feeds data into the Zepp app, which provides useful training features like VO2 max, recovery time, and a BioCharge energy metric (similar to Garmin’s Body Battery).

It’s let down by unreliable automatic workout detection and a Zepp Health app that can feel cluttered, but these are forgivable quirks. For anyone looking for a screenless, data-driven experience at a one-off price of just $99.00, the Helio Strap is an easy recommendation.

Check out our full Amazfit Helio Strap review
PROS:
Can be worn on the wrist and arm (with optional arm strap)
Good heart rate tracking accuracy across exercises
Useful training features (though not massively original)
CONS:
Automatic exercise recognition is overly sensitive
Zepp Health UI could be slicker
Only available in one color
Polar Loop (Gen 2)
(Image credit: Wareable)

Try Polar Loop (Gen 2) Now

Polar Loop (Gen 2) in brief:
Subscription-free alternative
Slim, comfortable fabric design optimized for 24/7 wear
Reliable sleep and recovery insights via Nightly Recharge and SleepWise
Best for existing Polar users who want a discreet way to track recovery

Polar Loop (Gen 2) marks the return of a legacy nameplate, redesigned to compete directly with screenless heavyweights like WHOOP.

Its primary appeal is financial: unlike WHOOP or Oura, there’s no mandatory monthly subscription. You pay a one-off fee for the hardware and get full access to the Polar Flow platform.

In our testing, Loop proved to be one of the most comfortable trackers we’ve worn. Similar to Hume Band 2.0, it’s slim and features a soft, knitted fabric band that disappears on the wrist.

For athletes who already own a Polar watch and simply want a more comfortable device for sleep tracking, Loop is a solid complement to your main tracker.

Software and accuracy trade-offs

However, the experience is hampered by the Polar Flow app, which—unlike the bespoke dashboards of Hume Health, Oura, or WHOOP—feels dated and unoptimized for a screenless device. Because there’s no display on the band, the app has to do all the heavy lifting, and, currently, it feels a bit clunky for those just wanting a quick glance at their recovery scores.

Accuracy is also a mixed bag. While the sleep data and Nightly Recharge metrics are top-tier and consistent with Oura Ring 4, the heart rate sensor (Polar’s older Precision Prime tech) can struggle during high-intensity intervals.

Unlike WHOOP or the Amazfit Helio Strap, Polar also doesn’t offer a bicep band accessory, which is a missed opportunity to improve accuracy. Still, for steady-state workouts and for holistic wellness without a subscription, Loop is a flawed-but-solid contender in 2026.

PROS:
Premium, slim, and comfortable design
No monthly subscription required
Reliable sleep tracking insights
CONS:
Polar Flow app feels dated and unoptimized for screenless use
Struggles with heart rate accuracy and workout detection
No bicep band option to improve accuracy
Xiaomi Smart Band 10
(Image credit: Wareable)

Try Xiaomi Smart Band 10

Xiaomi Smart Band 10 in brief:
Pebble Mode and accessories enable wear on a shoe, wrist, or as a necklace
16-day battery life (7 days with AOD enabled in our testing)
1.62-inch AMOLED display
5ATM water rating and IP68 water resistance
Tracks workouts, heart rate, stress, steps, and health metrics

Xiaomi Smart Band 10 retains its unique alternative wearing options thanks to its Pebble Mode.

This allows you to remove the sensor pod from its strap and place it in different accessories. You can wear the Smart Band 10 on your shoelaces to get running form metrics like cadence and strike pattern, or as a necklace pendant for discreet, all-day step counting.

This versatility is its key strength, but it comes with a significant trade-off. When worn as a pendant or the sold-separately shoe clip, it is no longer in contact with your skin.

This means you will lose all advanced tracking, and data such as heart rate, stress, and SpO2 monitoring are off-limits until you put it back on your wrist.

When on-wrist, it’s a fantastic basic tracker with a bright screen and incredible battery life for its low price. The data isn’t as accurate as Fitbit’s, but its value is unmatched.

PROS:
Battery life is unnecessarily good
Popping display and neat design
HR tracking data is very respectable
CONS:
Most sleep and health data isn’t accurate (or useful)
Still lacking built-in GPS
Fitbit Inspire 3
(Image credit: Wareable)

Try Fitbit Inspire 3

Fitbit Inspire 3 in brief
It can be worn on the wrist or clipped onto clothing via an official accessory
Works with Android and iOS
Up to 10 days of battery life
Tracks sleep, steps, calorie burn, workouts, and basic health metrics
Doesn’t have built-in GPS, but can harness a phone for distance tracking

Inspire 3 is a classic fitness tracker primarily worn on the wrist, but you can purchase an extra accessory to clip it to clothing. The clip enables you to secure Inspire 3 to the waistband of your trousers, a belt, or a bra.

However, just like with Xiaomi Smart Band 10, be aware of the trade-off. There is no heart rate data when clipped, so you’ll forgo in-depth wellness features.

You’ll still get access to basic features, including inactivity alerts and phone notifications. Inspire 3 offers Fitbit’s best battery life, with 10 days achievable between charges.

It costs a little more than Smart Band 10, but the excellent, motivating Google Health app makes it worth the extra cost.

A final thing to keep in mind is that this device is now getting pretty old and is a good candidate to be replaced by a newer tracker in 2026.

Check out our full Fitbit Inspire 3 review
PROS:
Powerful health/fitness features
A good-looking band
Brilliant battery life
CONS:
Double the price of budget options
Small screen
Garmin Lily 2
(Image credit: Wareable)

Try Garmin Lily 2 Now

Garmin Lily 2 in brief:
Small hybrid with a focus on fashion and health tracking
Offers sleep monitoring, cycle info, and activity tracking
Provides smart notifications and is compatible with iOS and Android
Features a patterned, low-res monochrome display
Battery life of up to 5 days

For those who want their tracking wrapped in a stylish, jewelry-like package, Garmin Lily 2 delivers. This 34mm watch suits smaller wrists and blends into everyday wear, making it one of the most discreet options available. It’s probably not strictly a hybrid, but it fits this section and guide well.

It excels in the basics—step counting, heart rate tracking, stress monitoring, and Garmin’s useful Body Battery feature—but lacks more advanced features like built-in GPS, so runners and cyclists will need to stay connected to their phones for accurate distance tracking.

Sleep and women’s health tracking are also included. They don’t quite match the depth found in Garmin’s higher-end models, but we think it’s still more than enough for those looking for a device with hidden smarts. They will be mostly hidden, as the patterned monochrome display hides stylishly when inactive. It isn’t the most vibrant or responsive compared to full-fledged watches, but it’s perfect for blending in.

If you want a fitness tracker that looks like jewelry first and a smartwatch second, this is one of the best options in 2026.

Check out our full Garmin Lily 2 review
PROS:
Elegant and lightweight design
Good set of fitness and health features
Decent accuracy
Body Battery and stress tracking are great
CONS:
No built-in GPS
Low-resolution, monochrome display
Average women’s health tracking
Sleep tracking could be improved
Bottom line

There is no single best screenless fitness tracker for everyone. The right choice depends on your lifestyle, health goals, and how much data you want from your wearable.

If you want the most complete wellness insights, choose Oura Ring 4. However, if you want similar smart ring benefits without a subscription, RingConn Gen 2 is an excellent alternative, with long battery life and a strong focus on sleep tracking.

Hume Band 2.0 is a great choice for beginners who prefer simple, guided wellness insights without being overwhelmed by data. For serious athletes who want deeper recovery and training metrics, WHOOP 5.0 remains one of the most advanced screenless wearables available.

Ultimately, the best choice comes down to your priorities: detailed health insights, all-day comfort, battery life, or simplicity.

 The best Garmin watches for training and everyday life
 Garmin may be best known for its hardcore fitness watches, but it’s got an extensive line of lifestyle offerings, too.

 Follow See All by Victoria Song 
 is a senior reporter and author of the Optimizer newsletter. She has more than 13 years of experience reporting on wearables, health tech, and more. Before coming to The Verge, she worked for Gizmodo and PC Magazine. 
 Few brands are as synonymous with outdoor sports as Garmin. You’ll find these fitness trackers and smartwatches on dozens of wrists at any 5K, marathon, or Ironman. You’ll also find Garmin devotees among divers, thru-hikers, golfers, kiteboarders — you name it. But these devices aren’t just for athletes. The company’s made significant strides in its lifestyle offerings, so regardless of your fitness level, there’s a Garmin for everyone.
 If you’re coming from a more traditional smartwatch, Garmin’s core strengths lie in fitness, GPS, adventuring, and durability. These are hardy devices that are meant to withstand the elements and last weeks on a single charge. Several models come with offline maps, advanced navigational features, and more training metrics than any other platform. Garmin devices tend to be on the pricier side, and the company announced in March 2025 that it would begin putting its newest features behind a paywall. That’s a bummer given Garmin spent years publicly stating it had no intention of charging its users extra.

 What we’re looking for
 How we test Garmin watches
 There are fitness trackers and smartwatches, and then there are Garmins. Depending on the type of Garmin — there are many — we will tailor our benchmarks and experiential, real-life testing. If it’s a rugged Fenix model, we’ll go on extensive GPS activities, see how well it works as a navigation tool, and dive deep into training metrics. If it’s more lifestyle focused, like the Venu 3 or Venu 4, we’ll put an added focus on how well smart features like voice assistant access, notifications, and style. Because people buy Garmins to last a long time, we also put special consideration on battery life testing. Some other factors we consider are durability, performance, ability to connect to gym equipment, and GPS accuracy.
 Battery life
 Garmins are known for extra long battery life. The question is, does it last days, weeks, or even a month?
 Training metrics
 Garmin has so many training features that even the pros probably don’t use all of them. Do you get coaching programs and stamina graphs? Or are you sticking to the basics like steps, pace, and mileage?
 Navigational features
 Same goes for navigational features. While Garmin is known for its GPS tech, there are multiple kinds of GPS tracking and satellite systems. We also look at whether these navigational features fit the use case. For example, do running watches have back-to-start? Do offline maps come preloaded for thru-hikers?
 Style and durability
 Do these watches hold up to intense activity? Are they discreet enough to wear to formal occasions without screaming “I love exercise!!!!”
 Value
 Garmins are expensive. Does the price make sense for the intended user, feature set, and build quality?
 Garmins aren’t too shabby on smarts, either. While more fitness-focused than anything from Apple, Google, or Samsung, there’s enough to get you the basics like notifications and then some. For example, most Garmins have fall detection and safety features, and several Garmins released since 2023 have an FDA-cleared EKG feature . (You’ll need a phone on hand, however, as only one Garmin model has cellular connectivity.) Many Garmin devices also support offline music playback and come with a small third-party app ecosystem.
 There are a lot of Garmin watches to choose from. No, seriously, there are six major lineups, and each has a multitude of models. But no worries — I test several Garmins every year and can help point you in the right direction.

 Garmin has many running watches, and a lot of them are great. But the Forerunner 265 or 265S (if you have petite wrists) strikes an excellent balance between price, feature set, and battery life. Its vibrant OLED display also impressed us. We got about a week on a single charge with always-on display enabled, and up to 15 days with that setting turned off.
 The 42mm Forerunner 265S fits on my petite wrists well. Plus, it’s lightweight, so it won’t distract you while running. Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge 
 The 265 has dual-frequency GPS (also known as multi-band), which gets you get much more accurate maps in challenging environments like cities and dense forests because you can access both the L1 and L5 satellite frequencies. You don’t lose a whole lot of battery life with dual-frequency GPS enabled. I wore it during a half marathon with that and the AOD enabled, and I still had over 80 percent battery by the time I got home. This is also an excellent price, as the majority of multi-band GPS watches cost well over $600.

 My main complaint is that $450 (outside of a deal, at least), while not bad for Garmin, is still a lot when you consider that’s the same price as smarter smartwatches with great running features. Some runners won’t care. But if you’re on a budget — or you’re new to running and feel iffy about spending that much — then consider the Forerunner 165 series. It starts at $249.99 (add another $50 for onboard music) and does almost everything the 265 series does. The main things you’re missing are dual-frequency GPS and a few more niche sport profiles. But if you’re mostly sticking to running, gym equipment, cycling, swimming, and hiking, you’re covered.
 Garmin Forerunner 165 Music

 Neither has all of Garmin’s training features, but it’s got what you’ll need to run anything from a 5K to a full marathon. That includes a Race Predictor, which gives you an estimate of what your best time would be based on your actual training. You can also use PacePro to figure out your pacing strategy for a race. You also get Garmin’s Training Readiness feature to help gauge load and recovery, Garmin Coach plans, and a host of running form metrics. It also supports offline music and safety features like fall detection. The only thing they lack is advanced mapping. (They still have trackback, point-to-point navigation, and real-time breadcrumb trail support, however.)
 On the other hand, if your budget allows, you could also consider the Forerunner 570 and Forerunner 970 , which were released in June and cost $549.99 and $749.99 , respectively. Both models have a built-in speaker and microphone, OLED screen, skin temperature sensors, flashlight, and built-in EKG reader with atrial fibrillation detection. They also give you a daily evening report with suggestions on how much sleep you should get, plus a digest of your upcoming events, workouts, and the weather. You also get access to Garmin Coach, a free multipart workout program, which allows you to upload your course and receive notifications when you’ve hit certain distance benchmarks.
 While both smartwatches have a lot in common, they do have some key differences, the main being that the 970 has maps. The Forerunner 570 comes in 42mm and 47mm sizes, and Garmin says its battery lasts up to 10 or 11 days based on which model you pick (with the always-on display off.) The Forerunner 970 only comes in a 47mm size, and Garmin says it can last up to 15 days per charge. The Forerunner 970 also includes three exclusive metrics: running tolerance, running economy, and speed step loss.
 These three tools will give you a weekly maximum mileage recommendation (with the option to adjust it up or down), and assess running efficiency. The running economy and step speed loss features require Garmin’s $169.99 HRM 600 heart rate monitor.
 The Forerunner 570 is a definite step up from the Forerunner 265, but not a big enough leap to recommend it to everyone instead of that model, especially because it doesn’t offer offline maps. The Forerunner 970 may be overkill for all but the most avid runners, but it’s good to see Garmin continually adding features to the top of its line.

 The Epix Pro will get you most fitness features Garmin had to offer, plus topographical maps, turn-by-turn navigation, and more training metrics than even a seasoned triathlete would know what to do with.
 The Pro is more size-inclusive than the standard second-gen Epix , which only comes in 47mm. You can get the Pro in that size, too, but it also comes in 42mm and 51mm. This was a major complaint I had with the second-gen Epix, and you love to see companies actually take this sort of thing seriously. The best part is that the Pro models start at the same price as the regular Epix did. You’ll have to pay $100 extra for materials like titanium and sapphire crystal, but that’s also true of the standard Epix.

 How we rate and review products 
 That said, it muddies the waters if you’re trying to pick between the Epix Pro, Fenix 7 , Fenix 7 Pro , and now, the Fenix 8 . The main difference is that the Epix watches all have OLED displays. One reason I prefer OLED screens is that they’re much easier to read indoors — where most of us spend the majority of our time. The Fenix 7 series’ memory-in-pixel displays (plus solar charging if you opt for it) allow for weeks and weeks of charge, but the smallest Epix Pro can get around 10 days with normal usage. The 47mm and 51mm Pro models can go longer between charges due to bigger batteries, but I felt that the 42mm has enough juice to satisfy most use cases. Garmin also has so many battery-saving modes and options that I highly doubt this will ever be an issue.
 Related
 The best Fitbits for your fitness and health 
 The ugly Pebble 2 Duo is the smartwatch for me 
 Not helping matters is the fact that the Fenix 8 lets you choose between an OLED and an MIP display. You also get smart features like an onboard voice assistant, the ability to take calls from the wrist, and the Garmin Messenger app. The main problem is that the starting price is now $350 more (barring any deals) than the standard Fenix 7 and right about on par with the Epix Pro. My personal feeling is that the Fenix 8’s smart features are just okay and that you’re really not missing much by not having them. We also often see discounts on older models, so I would put on my bargain-hunting hat for a discounted Epix Pro or Fenix 7 Pro while inventory is still available.
 But really, the winning feature of the Epix Pro is the hands-free flashlight. It’s so useful in my day-to-day life, and all you have to do is double-press a button. It’s as bright as your smartphone, comes with a red light option if you want something easier on the eyes, and can act as a strobe in an emergency situation. The Fenix 7 Pro and 8 watches also have a flashlight, so a lot of this is going to come down to personal preference for the display, price, and whether you care about smart features.
 We haven’t had a chance to get our hands on it yet, but Garmin also recently announced the Fenix 8 Pro. The watch, which starts at $1,199.99, is available in 47mm and 51mm sizes with either an OLED or MicroLED display. All models feature LTE and satellite connectivity, which costs $7.99 a month and allows you to send text and voice messages through the Garmin Messenger app when your phone is unavailable. The expanded connectivity also enables LiveTrack location sharing and access to real-time weather forecasts, as well as SOS requests, which get routed to Garmin’s Response Center and emergency services in the event of an emergency.

 What I love most about the Vivomove Sport is that it doesn’t look like what most people expect from a Garmin. It’s a hybrid smartwatch, which means it looks like a regular watch but can track fitness and deliver notifications. Garmin’s hybrids are also unique in that they all use an OLED display that stays hidden until you need it.
 This is best suited for a casually active person who wants style and value in a lightweight package. Think wellness, more so than fitness. It gets you continuous heart rate monitoring and blood oxygen level monitoring, and can even provide abnormal heart rate alerts. You also get access to more in-depth metrics like respiration rate, fitness age, stress, and Body Battery, which is Garmin’s tool for visualizing how well-rested you are. For smart features, you get all the basics, like notifications, alarms, and timers.
 You can’t easily read a whole text on this hidden OLED display, but you will know who sent it and make an educated choice about whether you want to reach for your phone. Photo by Victoria Song / The Verge 
 The Sport isn’t quite as full-featured as some other Garmin watches you’ll find on this list. For instance, you’re giving up built-in GPS in favor of tethered GPS through your phone. There are no contactless payments, nor is there a microphone or speaker for taking calls on the wrist. But this is a budget pick, and you get a lot, considering this is an entry-level gadget that could pass for a Swatch at a glance.
 I don’t love that the battery life is short for a hybrid, at around three to four days. Even so, that’s still much better than what you’ll get on a recent Apple Watch or Android watch running Wear OS 5 or 6. If you’re willing to spend about $100 more , the $269.99 Vivomove Trend has more chic materials, gets you more screen real estate, and wireless Qi charging. Otherwise, this is a great lifestyle wearable that can serve as a classier alternative to your typical fitness band.

The swipe and tap gestures are still a little fiddly to use — which was also the case with the first-gen model — but the fresh design is a fun way to lightly monitor your fitness without bogging yourself down with notifications. Garmin also offers the Lily 2 Active , which adds a physical button, GPS, and support for more sports tracking for a starting price of $299.99 .
